slides.narration: Almost all the mass of every atom sits in its nucleus, a few femtometres across. In this part we look at what nuclei are made of, how their size depends on the number of nucleons, the extraordinary force that holds them together, and why a nucleus weighs less than the particles that make it. That missing mass is the source of nuclear energy.

slides.heading: Composition of the nucleus
slides.body_md: A nucleus contains **protons** (charge $+e$) and **neutrons** (no charge), together called **nucleons**.
bullets: **Atomic number** $Z$ = number of protons; **mass number** $A$ = number of nucleons; **neutron number** $N = A - Z$. Notation: ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$.
Atomic masses are measured in **unified atomic mass units**: $1\ \text{u} = \tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of a ¹²C atom $= 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.
$m_p = 1.007276$ u, $m_n = 1.008665$ u (the neutron, discovered by Chadwick in 1932, is slightly heavier).

rows: Same N = A − Z, different Z

visual.alt: Table defining isotopes, isobars and isotones with an example of each

slides.narration: Every nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, called nucleons. The atomic number Z counts the protons and fixes the element; the mass number A counts all the nucleons. Nuclear masses are measured in unified atomic mass units, one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-twelve atom. Nuclei with the same Z but different A are isotopes; with the same A but different Z, isobars; with the same neutron number, isotones.

slides.heading: Size of the nucleus
slides.body_md:
Scattering experiments show that the nuclear radius grows with mass number as
$$R = R_0 A^{1/3},\qquad R_0 \approx 1.2\ \text{fm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$$
bullets: So the **volume** $\propto R^3 \propto A$: each nucleon occupies about the same volume.
Uranium-238 has 60 times as many nucleons as helium-4 but is only about 3.9 times wider.

slides.narration: Measurements show that the radius of a nucleus is R nought times A to the power one third, with R nought about one point two femtometres. Cubing both sides, the volume is proportional to A: nucleons are packed like marbles in a bag, each taking the same space. That is why a uranium nucleus with sixty times as many nucleons as helium is only about four times as wide.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: size and density
slides.body_md: Find the radius of an iron-56 nucleus and the density of nuclear matter. (Take $R_0 = 1.2$ fm and the mass of a nucleon as 1 u $= 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.)
bullets: Step 1 — $R = 1.2 \times 56^{1/3} \approx 4.59$ fm.
Step 2 — $\rho = \dfrac{Am_u}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{1.66 \times 10^{-27}}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi(1.2 \times 10^{-15})^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg m$^{-3}$.
Meaning — A cancels: every nucleus has about the same density, roughly 10¹⁴ times that of water.

slides.narration: The cube root of fifty six is about three point eight three, so the iron nucleus has a radius of about four point six femtometres. For the density, the mass is A nucleon masses and the volume is four thirds pi R nought cubed times A, so A cancels. The density comes out at about two times ten to the seventeen kilograms per cubic metre. A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh about a billion tonnes.

slides.heading: The nuclear force
slides.body_md: Protons repel each other strongly at nuclear distances, yet nuclei hold together. The **nuclear force** between nucleons:
bullets: is **much stronger** than the electrostatic force at nuclear distances;
is **short-range**: strong attraction at about 1 fm, negligible beyond a few fm; it becomes **repulsive** below about 0.8 fm;
is **charge-independent**: p–p, n–n and p–n forces are nearly the same;
acts only between neighbouring nucleons (**saturation**).

functions.label: nuclear potential energy of two nucleons

visual.alt: Schematic potential energy of two nucleons against separation: strongly repulsive closer than about 0.8 femtometre, a deep attractive well with its minimum near 1 femtometre, and almost zero beyond about 3 femtometres
visual.caption: Attractive between about 0.8 fm and a few fm, repulsive at shorter range; negligible beyond a few fm (short range).

slides.narration: Two protons a femtometre apart repel each other with a force of over a hundred newtons, enormous for such tiny particles. Something stronger must hold them in. The nuclear force is very strong but acts only over a few femtometres. It pulls nucleons together near one femtometre and pushes them apart if they get closer than about point eight. It treats protons and neutrons alike.

slides.heading: Mass and energy
slides.body_md: Einstein: mass and energy are equivalent, $$E = mc^2$$ A mass of 1 u is equivalent to about 931.5 MeV.
bullets: In nuclear reactions, the **total mass–energy** is conserved; a decrease in mass appears as kinetic energy or radiation.

visual.alt: Flow: mass lost in a nuclear process appears as energy equal to the mass times c squared, carried away as kinetic energy or radiation

slides.narration: Einstein showed that mass itself is a form of energy, with E equal to m c squared. Because c squared is so large, a tiny mass corresponds to a huge energy. In nuclear physics it is convenient to remember that one atomic mass unit is equivalent to about nine hundred and thirty one point five mega electronvolts. In a nuclear reaction, any mass that disappears comes out as energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the energy equivalent of 1 u
slides.body_md: Show that 1 u is equivalent to about 931.5 MeV. (1 u $= 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, $c = 2.998 \times 10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, $e = 1.6022 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

visual.alt: Table of energy equivalents: one atomic mass unit about 931.5 megaelectronvolts, one kilogram nine times ten to the sixteen joules, one gram nine times ten to the thirteen joules

slides.narration: Multiply one atomic mass unit in kilograms by the speed of light squared to get about one point four nine times ten to the minus ten joule. Divide by the number of joules in one mega electronvolt, one point six times ten to the minus thirteen, and you get about nine hundred and thirty one point five. A single gram of matter, completely converted, would give nine times ten to the thirteen joules.

slides.heading: Mass defect and binding energy
slides.body_md:
A nucleus has **less mass** than its separate nucleons. The **mass defect** is
$$\Delta M = [Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n] - M_\text{nucleus}$$
The **binding energy** $E_b = \Delta M c^2$ is the energy needed to separate the nucleus into free nucleons (or released when it forms).
bullets: Using **atomic** masses, use $m_\text{H} = 1.007825$ u in place of $m_p$ so that the electrons cancel.
Binding energy per nucleon $E_{bn} = E_b/A$ measures how tightly the nucleons are held.

slides.narration: Weigh a helium nucleus and you find it is lighter than two protons and two neutrons weighed separately. This mass defect, times c squared, is the binding energy: the energy given out when the nucleus forms, and the energy you would have to supply to pull it apart. Dividing by the number of nucleons gives the binding energy per nucleon, the best measure of how stable a nucleus is.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: helium-4
slides.body_md: The atomic mass of $\,{}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ is 4.002603 u. Find its mass defect, binding energy and binding energy per nucleon. ($m_\text{H} = 1.007825$ u, $m_n = 1.008665$ u.)
bullets: Step 2 — $E_b = 0.03038 \times 931.5 \approx 28.3$ MeV.
Step 3 — $E_{bn} = \dfrac{28.3}{4} \approx 7.07$ MeV per nucleon.

slides.narration: Two hydrogen atoms and two neutrons have a total mass of four point zero three three atomic mass units, but a helium-four atom has only four point zero zero three. The difference, about point zero three zero four, times nine hundred and thirty one point five, is a binding energy of about twenty eight megaelectronvolts, or about seven megaelectronvolts per nucleon. Helium-four is unusually tightly bound for such a light nucleus.

slides.heading: The binding energy per nucleon curve
slides.body_md: Binding energy per nucleon against mass number:
bullets: Rises steeply for light nuclei (²H only 1.1 MeV); helium-4, carbon-12 and oxygen-16 stand out above the trend.
Roughly **constant at about 8 MeV** for 30 < A < 170, with a **peak of about 8.8 MeV** near A = 56 (iron).
Falls slowly for heavy nuclei to about 7.6 MeV for uranium.

slides.narration: Plot binding energy per nucleon against mass number and you get one of the most important graphs in physics. It rises steeply through the light nuclei, flattens out at about eight megaelectronvolts, peaks near iron at about eight point eight, and then falls gently to about seven point six for uranium. Nuclei near the peak are the most tightly bound and the most stable.

slides.heading: Reading the curve
slides.body_md: What the shape tells us:
bullets: **Nearly constant** $E_{bn}$ in the middle: each nucleon interacts only with its **neighbours** (short range, saturation).
Heavy nuclei: the long-range **Coulomb repulsion** of many protons lowers $E_{bn}$.
**Fission** of a heavy nucleus into two middle-sized ones, and **fusion** of light nuclei, both move towards the peak and so **release energy** (Part 2).

visual.alt: Binding energy per nucleon against mass number: it rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 megaelectronvolts near iron-56, then falls slowly to about 7.6 for uranium; points for deuterium, helium-4, lithium-7, carbon-12, oxygen-16, iron-56, krypton-92, barium-141, uranium-235 and uranium-238 are computed from their masses

slides.narration: If every nucleon attracted every other one, the binding energy per nucleon would keep growing with A. Instead it levels off, because each nucleon only feels its near neighbours. In heavy nuclei the electrical repulsion between many protons, which does act across the whole nucleus, pulls the curve down. Anything that moves nuclei towards the peak near iron releases energy.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: $R = R_0A^{1/3}$, $R_0 \approx 1.2$ fm; density ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ for all nuclei
Strong, short-range, charge-independent, repulsive below 0.8 fm
$E_b = \Delta M c^2$, $\Delta M = Zm_\text{H} + (A - Z)m_n - M$
Peak ≈ 8.8 MeV near A = 56; ≈ 7.6 MeV for U

visual.alt: Summary table of nuclear composition, size and density, the nuclear force, mass–energy equivalence, binding energy and the binding-energy curve

slides.narration: To sum up: a nucleus has Z protons and A minus Z neutrons, a radius R nought A to the one third, and the same huge density whatever its size. A strong, short-range nuclear force holds it together. Its mass is less than that of its nucleons, and the mass defect times c squared is the binding energy. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron at about eight point eight megaelectronvolts.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: With atomic masses, use $m_\text{H}$, not $m_p$, so electron masses cancel.
Keep 5–6 decimal places in mass sums; round only the final answer.
Convert with 1 u = 931.5 MeV; 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Sketch the BE curve with labelled peak (≈ 8.8 MeV, A ≈ 56) and say what it implies for fission and fusion.

slides.narration: Mass defect questions are easy marks if you are careful with decimals: keep all the digits until the end, and if you are given atomic masses, use the hydrogen atom mass so the electrons cancel. Remember the conversion, nine hundred and thirty one point five megaelectronvolts per atomic mass unit. And practise sketching the binding energy curve with its peak near iron.

slides.heading: Fission and fusion
slides.body_md: Part 2 — splitting heavy nuclei and joining light ones: the two ways to unlock nuclear energy.

visual.alt: Binding energy per nucleon against mass number: it rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 megaelectronvolts near iron-56, then falls slowly to about 7.6 for uranium; points for deuterium, helium-4, lithium-7, carbon-12, oxygen-16, iron-56, krypton-92, barium-141, uranium-235 and uranium-238 are computed from their masses

slides.narration: Look again at the binding energy curve. Heavy nuclei at the right and light nuclei at the left are both less tightly bound than those in the middle. So splitting a uranium nucleus releases energy, and so does joining two hydrogen nuclei. In this part we see how fission powers nuclear reactors, and how fusion powers the Sun.

slides.heading: Nuclear fission
slides.body_md:
A slow neutron absorbed by $\,{}^{235}\text{U}$ makes an unstable $\,{}^{236}\text{U}$ nucleus that splits into two medium-mass fragments and 2–3 neutrons, for example
$$\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{235}_{92}\text{U} \to {}^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + Q$$
bullets: Nucleon number and charge are conserved: $1 + 235 = 141 + 92 + 3$ and $92 = 56 + 36$.

slides.heading: Chain reaction and reactors
slides.body_md: The 2–3 neutrons from each fission can cause further fissions: a **chain reaction**.
bullets: **Uncontrolled** (each fission triggers more than one more): an explosion, as in an atom bomb.

**Controlled** (on average exactly one more): steady power in a **nuclear reactor**. A **moderator** (heavy water, graphite) slows the neutrons; **control rods** (cadmium, boron) absorb extra neutrons; a **coolant** carries the heat to turbines.
India runs pressurised heavy-water reactors, for example at Kaiga and Rawatbhata.

visual.alt: Flow of a controlled chain reaction: a neutron causes fission releasing two or three neutrons, the moderator slows them, control rods absorb the extras, giving steady power

slides.narration: Each fission releases two or three neutrons, and each of those can split another uranium nucleus. If every fission leads to more than one new fission, the reaction grows explosively. In a reactor it is held at exactly one: a moderator slows the neutrons so they are captured easily, and control rods soak up the extras. The heat is carried away to make steam and drive turbines.

slides.heading: Nuclear fusion
slides.body_md:
Light nuclei combine into a heavier, more tightly bound nucleus, for example
$$\,{}^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\text{H} \to {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + 17.6\ \text{MeV}$$
bullets: The nuclei must get within a few fm against their **Coulomb repulsion**: this needs temperatures of about $10^7$–$10^8$ K (**thermonuclear** fusion).
Per nucleon, fusion releases more energy than fission.

slides.heading: Fusion in the Sun
slides.body_md: In the Sun’s core (about $1.5 \times 10^7$ K), hydrogen fuses into helium through a chain of reactions, net:
bullets: $4\,{}^{1}\text{H} + 2e^- \to {}^{4}\text{He} + 2\nu + 6\gamma$, releasing about **26.7 MeV**.
The Sun converts about $4 \times 10^{9}$ kg of mass into energy every second.
Controlled fusion on Earth (tokamaks such as ITER, with India as a partner) is still being developed.

slides.narration: The Sun is a giant fusion reactor. In its core, at about fifteen million kelvin, hydrogen nuclei fuse step by step into helium, each complete cycle releasing about twenty seven megaelectronvolts. Every second the Sun turns about four billion kilograms of mass into energy. Scientists, including Indian teams working on the international ITER project, are trying to tame fusion on Earth.

slides.heading: Fission and fusion compared
slides.body_md: Both move nuclei towards the peak of the BE curve:
columns:
**Fission**
- Heavy nucleus splits
- Needs a slow neutron to start
- ≈ 200 MeV per event (≈ 0.9 MeV per nucleon)
- Radioactive waste

**Fusion**
- Light nuclei join
- Needs ~10⁷–10⁸ K
- 17.6 MeV per D–T event (≈ 3.5 MeV per nucleon)
- Little long-lived waste

visual.alt: Binding energy per nucleon against mass number: it rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 megaelectronvolts near iron-56, then falls slowly to about 7.6 for uranium; points for deuterium, helium-4, lithium-7, carbon-12, oxygen-16, iron-56, krypton-92, barium-141, uranium-235 and uranium-238 are computed from their masses
visual.caption: Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move towards the peak, so both release energy.

slides.narration: Fission splits heavy nuclei and is triggered by a slow neutron; fusion joins light ones and needs enormous temperatures. Fission gives more energy per event, but fusion gives more per nucleon, and so more per kilogram of fuel. Fission is used in power stations today; fusion powers the stars and may one day power our cities, with far less long-lived radioactive waste.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: energy from one gram of uranium-235
slides.body_md: Estimate the energy released if all the nuclei in 1.0 g of U-235 undergo fission, at 200 MeV each. ($N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$.)
bullets: Step 1 — $N = \dfrac{1.0}{235} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \approx 2.56 \times 10^{21}$ nuclei.
Step 2 — $E = 2.56 \times 10^{21} \times 200 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \approx 8.2 \times 10^{10}$ J.
Meaning — about the energy from burning 3 tonnes of coal.

sections.heading: 1. Composition and size of nuclei
sections.body_md:
- Nucleus: $Z$ protons and $N = A - Z$ neutrons (**nucleons**); notation ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$.
- **Isotopes:** same Z, different A. **Isobars:** same A, different Z. **Isotones:** same N.
- Masses in unified atomic mass units: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = $1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg; $m_p = 1.007276$ u, $m_n = 1.008665$ u, $m_\text{H} = 1.007825$ u.
- **Radius:** $R = R_0A^{1/3}$, $R_0 \approx 1.2$ fm. Volume ∝ A, so nuclear **density** is the same for all nuclei, about $2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg m⁻³.

sections.heading: 2. The nuclear force
sections.body_md:
- Holds nucleons together against the Coulomb repulsion of protons; **much stronger** than the electrostatic force at nuclear distances.
- **Short range:** strongly attractive around 1 fm, negligible beyond a few fm; **repulsive** below about 0.8 fm (so nuclei do not collapse).
- **Charge-independent:** p–p, n–n and n–p forces are about equal.
- **Saturation:** each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours.

sections.heading: 3. Mass–energy, mass defect and binding energy
sections.body_md:
- $E = mc^2$; 1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV; 1 MeV = $1.6 \times 10^{-13}$ J.
- **Mass defect:** $\Delta M = Zm_\text{H} + (A - Z)m_n - M_\text{atom}$ (with atomic masses).
- **Binding energy:** $E_b = \Delta M c^2 = \Delta M \times 931.5$ MeV/u: the energy to separate the nucleus into its nucleons.
- **Binding energy per nucleon** $E_{bn} = E_b/A$: about 7.07 MeV for ⁴He, 7.98 MeV for ¹⁶O, a **peak ≈ 8.8 MeV near A = 56**, about 7.6 MeV for ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U.
- Nearly constant $E_{bn}$ for 30 < A < 170 shows the short range (saturation) of the nuclear force; the fall for heavy nuclei is due to Coulomb repulsion.

Energy equivalent of the mass defect; energy needed to break the nucleus into free nucleons.

sections.heading: 4. Nuclear fission and fusion
sections.body_md:
- **Fission:** a heavy nucleus splits into two medium nuclei, e.g. $\text{n} + {}^{235}\text{U} \to {}^{141}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}\text{Kr} + 3\text{n}$; about **200 MeV** per fission (≈ 0.85 MeV per nucleon). The neutrons can sustain a **chain reaction**: uncontrolled in a bomb, controlled in a **reactor** (moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb them; coolant removes heat).
- **Fusion:** light nuclei join, e.g. $\,{}^{2}\text{H} + {}^{3}\text{H} \to {}^{4}\text{He} + \text{n} + 17.6$ MeV (≈ 3.5 MeV per nucleon). Needs $10^7$–$10^8$ K to overcome Coulomb repulsion (thermonuclear). Powers the Sun: net $4\,{}^{1}\text{H} \to {}^{4}\text{He}$ + 26.7 MeV.
- **Why both release energy:** the products lie nearer the **peak** of the BE-per-nucleon curve, so they are more tightly bound; the gain in total binding energy is released.
- $Q$ = (mass before − mass after) × 931.5 MeV/u = (total BE after − total BE before).

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The nuclear force is charge-independent: p–p, n–n and n–p nuclear forces are nearly equal (protons also repel electrically, but that is a separate force).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Nuclei do not collapse even though the nuclear force between nucleons is strongly attractive.

**Reason (R):** The nuclear force becomes repulsive when nucleons come closer than about 0.8 fm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the repulsive core keeps nucleons apart, so nuclear matter has a fixed density — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State four properties of the nuclear force.

answer.model_answer_md: Any four: it is **much stronger** than the electrostatic force at nuclear distances; it is **short-range** (negligible beyond a few fm); it is **charge-independent** (p–p, n–n, n–p nearly equal); it is **attractive** at about 1 fm but **repulsive** below about 0.8 fm; it **saturates** (acts only between neighbouring nucleons).

questions.solution_md: Four properties.

questions.stem_md: Find the electrostatic force of repulsion between two protons 1.5 fm apart in a nucleus, in newtons (3 significant figures). (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².)
questions.solution_md: $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(1.5 \times 10^{-15})^2} \approx 102$ N: a huge force on such tiny particles, which the nuclear force must overcome.

options.text_md: ³₁H and ³₂He

¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O

questions.stem_md: Using R = R₀A^(1/3), show that the density of a nucleus does not depend on its mass number, and estimate its value for R₀ = 1.2 fm. (Mass of a nucleon ≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.)

answer.model_answer_md: Mass $M \approx Am$, volume $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$. So $\rho = \dfrac{Am}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{m}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3}$: **A cancels**, so all nuclei have the same density. Numerically $\rho = \dfrac{1.66 \times 10^{-27}}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi(1.2 \times 10^{-15})^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg m$^{-3}$.

questions.solution_md: Mass ∝ A, volume ∝ A.

questions.stem_md: Define mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus. How are they related?

answer.model_answer_md: The **mass defect** is the difference between the total mass of the **separate nucleons** and the mass of the **nucleus**. The **binding energy** is the energy needed to **separate** the nucleus into its nucleons (equal to the energy released when it forms). They are related by $E_b = \Delta M c^2$, i.e. $\Delta M \times 931.5$ MeV/u.

questions.solution_md: Definitions and E = Δm c².

marking_scheme.step: Binding energy defined and E_b = ΔMc²

questions.stem_md: Sketch (describe) the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number. State two features of the graph and one conclusion drawn from each.

answer.model_answer_md: The curve rises steeply for light nuclei, is roughly **flat at about 8 MeV** for 30 < A < 170, **peaks at about 8.8 MeV near A = 56** and **falls slowly** to about 7.6 MeV for uranium. (1) Flat middle → the nuclear force is **short-range** and saturates. (2) Lower values at both ends → **fusion** of light nuclei and **fission** of heavy nuclei both move towards the peak and **release energy**.

questions.solution_md: Shape; flatness → short range; ends → fission and fusion.

marking_scheme.step: Correct shape with peak ≈ 8.8 MeV near A = 56
Feature and conclusion: fission/fusion release energy

questions.stem_md: Why is the binding energy per nucleon nearly constant for nuclei with mass numbers between about 30 and 170?

answer.model_answer_md: The nuclear force is **short-range**: each nucleon is attracted only by its **nearest neighbours**, not by all the nucleons. Adding more nucleons adds about the **same** binding for each one (**saturation**), so the binding energy per nucleon stays nearly constant instead of growing with A.

questions.solution_md: Short range, saturation.

marking_scheme.step: Each nucleon bound only to neighbours (short range)
So E_b ∝ A, E_bn nearly constant

questions.stem_md: The function of the moderator (such as heavy water or graphite) in a nuclear reactor is to

options.text_md: absorb all the neutrons
slow down the fast neutrons produced in fission
speed up the neutrons
cool the reactor core

questions.solution_md: Slow (thermal) neutrons are far more likely to cause fission of U-235, so the moderator slows them — option (b).

options.text_md: absorb neutrons strongly
